title: Brotherhood and Heartbreak on the Utah Backcountry Discovery Route – Karter Machen, Chris Burkard, Lachlan Morton, Mateo Paez, & Nate Sorenson
content:
Lachlan Morton, Chris Burkard, Mateo Páez, Karter Machen, and Nate Sorenson experience the BDR together and recount the story from their own angle, from hard desert logistics to a first-time bikepacker’s shift from feeling out of his depth to pure joy. Pedaling nearly 800 miles from Evanston, Wyoming, to Monument Valley over ten days, each rider shares in the lesson that the people you travel with matter more than the place, and life can bring joy and sorrow in equal measure. Join the trip…

Lachlan

When the 6-minute voice message from Nate came through on WhatsApp, I knew he wasn’t interested in abandoning his north-south Utah route to join me on the Sierra Foothills route I’d put together. Upon listening to his explanation, I knew my route would have to wait. There was no question I’d be joining him on his mission.

Nate is one of my best mates. We met in Albania when he was capturing the action behind the camera, documenting the journey. In the years since, he has captured a lot of my longer rides. He has witnessed the raw reality of these efforts, the ugly parts, the parts that won’t make the cut when you’re in the business of romanticizing. But for whatever reason, this only fueled a fire within him to experience that for himself. He picked up his bike, built his fitness, and gained experience slowly. We’d done a couple of trips together in the saddle and even when we were having the greatest time, he was also taking notes, honing his experience in on something that was coming. I now knew this was it; this is what he was building toward. There was no way I could miss this. This was a celebration of the beautiful place he came from and the life he wants to lead, with no meat left on the bone.

The route itself intrigued me. Essentially, we’d be hopping between mountain ranges as we made our way south. These ‘small’ ranges would all be mountains of note where I grew up, but in the States they are shadowed by the grander peaks and divides that neighbor them. The mountains wouldn’t pose the biggest challenge – at higher elevations the temperature would be pleasant and the streams flowing. It was the dry, hot expanses that linked them that would provide the biggest obstacle.

The crew assembled was a list of guys I feel lucky to have as mates. Friendships this tight are easily bonded in childhood, when we’re more open, curious, and accepting. These friendships I have made as an adult, and as I get older, I’ve realized that is something special. With this group I could feel not only myself, but an open, capable, and free version that is only available to me when I feel completely comfortable. Both Chris and Karter I’d shared many miles with. Friends through chance, but forged in situations where true character is exposed and therefore, in this case, ensuring a lifelong bond. Mateo was new to me, but only in the sense that we hadn’t met. Of the same age, with wildly different paths in cycling, we shared an instant and deep connection on this route. As a child and adolescent, I took myself quite seriously, and due to that, I feel I missed my true band of brothers. The kind of friends that get into trouble, laugh, and hold each other accountable. With this group I found that, and there was no one else I’d rather be on the journey with.

Whilst we made good pace, calculated water carries and had our resupplies locked in, there was never any hesitation to stop and jump in a river, make some peanut butter tortillas, or fire up the burner for a coffee. We travelled over a vast distance, but none of it was lost on us; we took it all in. There was an unspoken knowing that for us, this is what life is truly about, and we soaked in every moment.

Deep into the trip, I noticed a look in Nate’s eyes that was familiar to me. A man on the edge of his physical capability, wringing the towel dry. The only difference between what I have experienced in this moment and the way he was experiencing it was that he never for a second let it diminish what he was experiencing. He had a presence of mind that ensured he knew that’s what he was there for, and having reached it, he wasn’t going to shy away from that experience for a second.

My takeaway from this trip was simply to make time to go sleep in the dirt with your mates. Our modern lives make it all too easy to be too busy. But for me now it feels a lot clearer. These experiences take commitment; you have to make the time, cut some ambition, and allow yourself to be that kid who just wants to go ride bikes with his friends. I came away from this trip with not only a cup full of renewed motivation and ideas but a greater appreciation for the experience we can have just viewing the world that exists around us and how much better that is when you share it with mates.

Mateo

We met up with the boys at mile 102 in Evanston, Wyoming. It was the second Friday in June. If you follow bikepacking or ultra racing in general, you know this date is an important one. I was more than glad to be out on the road again, loaded bike, not racing, and staring down the vast expanse of the Great Basin on this particular day.

Joining an 800-mile, statewide crossing of a bikepacking trip with strangers is a questionable decision. I have ridden with Chris enough to trust him. We have grown to become close friends through bikepacking. Meeting in Iceland, riding the Monumental Loop, packrafting in Utah, and always scheming something 12 months out of the year. I think I can trust Lachlan’s ability to handle himself in the backcountry. Karter, well, he’s been vouched for by the rest of them. Nate is a total gem of a rad dad and a historian of his home state of Utah. I just met him too. Simple as that, Nate wanted to ride across Utah, and I was lucky enough to be invited as a pre-approved stranger.

I never doubted our ability as a group but quickly learned that this is a huge deal for two of the 5 guys. For Karter, this is his first off-road bikepacking trip. First time riding a mountain bike, and on a borrowed one at that. For Nate, this might be his fifth bikepacking trip? I sure couldn’t tell without them telling me. Their setups are dialed, confidence is oozing, and we have a lot of rugged country to get through. I just assumed that if these guys can hang with Lach then we were good to go. As the days went on, I was thrilled to share anything that I know to help our fellow road dogs get to the end of this route.

We had daily goals; those turned into which petroglyphs to stop and see. This wasn’t all easy miles and casual resupplies, though. It took some calculated planning to make sure we could make it through some long desert stretches. Those stretches meant leaving at 4:00 am and taking long midday swim sessions in the Green and Colorado Rivers. A few big passes were joyous at elevation, but once we were in canyon country, I felt locked into a maze of sand, impassable cliffs, and heat.

A common thread among all of us: this appetite for slowing down. Bikepacking, my way of slowing down while constantly trying to speed up. Exploring new and familiar places, tying together once-traveled regions by bike with a new perspective. It gives me time and space to feel the landscape. It takes exposure to the elements for a couple of days, sleeping on the ground and waking up excited to eat at the gas station. Bikepacking is always hard at some point; it doesn’t matter where or how fast you ride, the challenge is part of it and the experience is always worth it.

I made it to day 7 of the 10. Then I had to get back to work in Oregon and catch a flight.

I left the boys at 4:00 am somewhere in the La Sal Range. I rode myself to Moab that morning, descending by the Fisher Towers at sunrise. It was bittersweet leaving them, knowing the hardest days were ahead and I wouldn’t be able to see my trusted road dogs make it to Monument Valley, the end of the line. As the days wore us down physically, our guards were stripped away. We strangers became bonded through overland travel, slowly but surely. Throughout this journey, I lost a friend to a drunk driver. She was hit while cycling home from dinner. I received the news midway through our ride. I didn’t talk about it much other than to Chris because it’s horribly sad and, to be honest, it hurt too much. Someone so bright, taken so swiftly doing something so simple, just riding home. On day four, Chris received a call that one of his close friends passed away in an accident doing something they love, someone we were with a month prior. This sparked quite a somber moment amongst all five of us in a shitty motel room in the middle of nowhere.

The harshest of reminders that these things we love – cycling, traveling, experiencing hardships and tailwinds – are better together with trusted friends who motivate you to be more than just a reliable travel partner on the bike. We inspire each other to be good humans.

Karter

When Nate, the man behind the route, first told me about the idea months before we left, I couldn’t quite wrap my head around it. Crossing Utah from north to south by mountain bike sounded equal parts ridiculous and intriguing. I agreed almost immediately.
At first it was just the two of us. Over the following months Lachlan, Chris, and Mateo joined the plan, and before long I found myself riding alongside people I’d admired for years. I was, without question, the least experienced of the group, and I felt completely out of my depth.

Then the first day arrived.

As soon as we started pedaling, most of that fear disappeared. I had some idea of what lay ahead – the terrain, the heat, the long days – but I had no idea the trip would become one of the most joyful and impactful experiences of my life.

Over the following days, each of the guys generously shared years of hard-earned knowledge, advice, and wisdom, always with a willingness to lend a hand when it was needed. I’d spent plenty of time riding with Lachlan and Nate over the years, and they’ve become two of my closest friends through our travels, but this was my first time getting to know Mateo and Chris. It didn’t take long to understand how I was in good company.

I thought I knew Utah, but man, was I wrong.

Moving through the state at the pace of a bicycle revealed an intimate version I’d never experienced before. The iconic red desert, alpine meadows, and high mountain passes before dropping us back into a heat so relentless and unforgiving that it’s almost impossible to describe. It’s something you simply have to experience.

There was something deeply satisfying about living by the rhythm of the sun, sleeping on the ground, cooling off in rivers whenever we found them, and watching the Milky Way stretch across the night sky. Those moments were unforgettable.

But when I look back now, it’s not the landscapes or the effort; it’s the time spent and connections made with such a good group of guys.

Life doesn’t stop simply because you’re on an adventure. During those ten days, some of us received heartbreaking news from home. Others, myself included, were quietly working through difficult seasons of life. We all carried something.

I’m grateful for the hours we spent together, for the climbs that turned into conversations, the swims that washed away the day’s heat, swollen eyes over morning coffees in dry washes, and the peanut butter and honey tortillas Lach graciously had prepared up the climbs. Those simple moments gave us the space to show up for one another.

More than an expedition across Utah, it became a reminder that the places we travel are often only half the story. It’s the people you experience them with.
